raw_response:
Use separate terminology for two properties: a shared or aliasable reference describes access, while the trait describes whether concurrent access through such references is safe. Interior mutation must remain allowed when the type's safe interface coordinates it correctly.

1. JSR-305's ThreadSafe and Immutable annotations — https://chromium.googlesource.com/external/jsr-305/+/151fd3976210c6b79117e30b02aee86a20ff5c7f/ri/src/main/java/javax/annotation/concurrent/ThreadSafe.java

   This is the strongest direct naming precedent: concurrency safety has its own ThreadSafe label, separate from Immutable. The contract concerns preserving valid object state under interleaved public accesses without additional caller coordination. For Rust, explicitly restrict the adapted meaning to safe concurrent access through shared references; Java's broad object-level promise should not silently become a guarantee about ownership transfer or every possible operation. The opened 2008-08-25 source diff establishes both labels before the cutoff: https://chromium.googlesource.com/external/jsr-305/+/4e1f9dc708a57e175e76833b0d1b27212b74d0c5%5E!/

2. Qt's reentrant versus thread-safe distinction — https://doc.qt.io/Archives/qt-4.7/threads-reentrancy.html

   Qt separates concurrent use of different instances from concurrent use of the same instance. This helps state exactly what the trait adds beyond ordinary access and shows why Reentrant would be an insufficient replacement. Its example also uses an internally mutable mutex inside a const accessor, making the distinction from literal immutability concrete. The locking example is illustrative; the Rust trait must not require a particular synchronization mechanism. This is archived Qt 4.7.0 documentation with a 2008-2010 footer.

3. Reference-immutability and isolation qualifiers for safe parallelism — https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/publication/uniqueness-and-reference-immutability-for-safe-parallelism/

   This October 2012 paper distinguishes writable, readable, immutable, and isolated references, then separately specifies when those references permit safe parallel execution. That separation is useful as a design model: naming an access capability does not automatically establish concurrent-sharing safety. The paper's readable views can coexist with writable aliases elsewhere, while immutable adds a stronger restriction. However, readable forbids mutation through that reference, so it is not an equivalent replacement for Rust shared access with interior mutability. The linked extended paper was opened and its qualifier definitions checked.

4. Boost shared_ptr's ownership vocabulary and separate concurrency contract — https://www.boost.org/doc/libs/1_55_0/libs/smart_ptr/shared_ptr.htm

   Boost uses shared to describe lifetime/ownership and gives thread-safety rules separately. That supports keeping shared reference as ordinary terminology without implying that every shared object is safe for simultaneous access. The documentation distinguishes concurrent const accesses to a pointer instance from mutations of different pointer instances and from unsafe simultaneous operations. Reference-count safety does not make arbitrary pointee operations safe, and shared ownership is not identical to a borrowed reference. The opened version is Boost 1.55.0, identified on the page as a 2013 release.

5. Chromium's ThreadSafe suffix — https://www.chromium.org/developers/coding-style/important-abstractions-and-data-structures/

   RefCountedThreadSafe and ObserverListThreadSafe are concrete naming examples in which an explicit concurrency qualifier supplements an ownership or collection term. This suggests a name that identifies the safety property directly while leaving shared/aliasable access terminology alone. The guarantee must stay scoped to the relevant operations; a safe reference counter does not imply that all reachable object state is safe. The opened source is live documentation, so availability of this evidence before the cutoff is unknown.

6. D's thread-shared versus thread-local vocabulary — https://dlang.org/faq.html

   D explicitly associates shared with cross-thread visibility and contrasts it with unshared/thread-local data. This offers vocabulary for explaining the concurrency dimension independently of whether multiple aliases exist in one thread. It also provides a useful caution: the FAQ separately discusses synchronization and says the qualifier does not automatically insert memory barriers. Therefore D's shared qualifier is not a drop-in semantic equivalent of the Rust trait. The live FAQ redirected to https://dlang.org/articles/faq.html; its historical availability was not established.

The closest established naming family is ThreadSafe, provided the trait documentation preserves the exact predicate: concurrent use of shared references to the value is safe, including any permitted interior mutation. A more explicit spelling such as ThreadShareSafe would be a new naming suggestion derived from these precedents, not an existing standard claimed by these sources. Immutable, ReadOnly, Reentrant, or Atomic would each imply a different property.
